# Sela Sutta (MN 92 (PTS MN ii 146))

**ID:** MN 92 (PTS MN ii 146)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Sela Sutta  
**Title (English, from literature):** With Sela  
**PTS:** MN ii 146  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul4.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul4.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sela Sutta* (MN 92) recounts the conversion of the brahmin Sela and his assembly of pupils [Anālayo 2017]. In the narrative framework, the ascetic Keṇiya prepares an elaborate meal for the Buddha and the Saṅgha [Katre 1931]. Observing these preparations, the brahmin Sela approaches the Buddha and inspects him for the thirty-two bodily marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa*) [Kingsbury 2002]. When the Buddha miraculously reveals the two marks that are concealed—his tongue and his sheath-covered private parts—Sela is convinced and extols the Buddha in verse [Anālayo 2017; Kingsbury 2002; Katre 1931]. Urging the Buddha to rule as a universal monarch or "king of kings" (*rājābhirāja*), Sela hears the Buddha declare his spiritual kingship as the Dhamma-king; Sela and his followers subsequently go forth and attain arahantship [Endo 1997; Anālayo 2017].

Scholars have given particular attention to the literary composition and transmission of the discourse. The text is virtually identical to the sutta of the same name found in the *Sutta Nipāta* (Snp 3.7) [Kingsbury 2002; Winternitz 1933]. Because of this complete duplication, English translations of the Majjhima Nikāya note that page citations embedded in MN 92 sometimes refer to the PTS pagination of the *Sutta Nipāta* [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The verses are also preserved in the *Theragāthā* (Thag 16.6) as the *Selattheragāthā* [Endo 1997]. S. M. Katre identified the sutta as a composite work fusing the prose story of Keṇiya—also found in the Vinaya's *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* (Kd 6)—with twenty-four additional stanzas containing the dialogue with Sela [Katre 1931]. In Sanskrit Buddhist literature, the text was known as the *Śailagāthā* and was counted among the preserved poetic collections, as evidenced by citations in the *Divyāvadāna* [Lamotte 1988; Hazra 1994].

 Full and partial parallels exist in Snp 3.7, the Vinaya *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* (Kd 6), the Chinese Vinaya (*dg-kd7*), the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu* (*lo-mvu108*), the *Ekottarika-āgama* (EĀ 49.6), and the *Itivuttaka* (Iti 100). In comparative studies, Anālayo notes that the *Ekottarika-āgama* parallel to the sutta illustrates the mark of the retractile organ with the comparison to a king of horses, explaining it as a symbol of chastity and purity [Anālayo 2017].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: Snp 3.7 (PTS Snp 102) Sela Sutta
- Passage-level parallels: Lzh Dg Kd 7 Bhesajja Khandhaka; Kd 6 Bhesajjakkhandhaka; EA 49.6; Thag 16.6 Selattheragāthā; Snp 3.6 (PTS Snp 91) Sabhiya Sutta; San Lo Mvu 108 The Three Kāśyapas
- Resembling parallels: SF 12; Iti 100 (It 4.1 PTS It 101) Brāhmaṇadhammayāga Sutta
- Mentioned in: Pe 2 Sāsanapaṭṭhānadutiyabhūmi; Mil 5.3.10 Vaṇṇabhaṇanapañha; Mil 5.5.8 Brāhmaṇarājavādapañha

**Sources**

- [Endo 1997] Toshiichi Endo, Buddha in Theravada Buddhism: A Study of the Concept of Buddha in the Pali Commentaries (1997) — Discussed the title rājābhirāja in the Sela Sutta and its repetition in MN, Snp, and Thag.
- [Anālayo 2017] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Buddhapada and the Bodhisattva Path (2017) — Analyzed Sela's verification of the 32 marks, tongue display, ordination, and the horse simile in the Ekottarika-āgama parallel.
- [Kingsbury 2002] Paul Kingsbury, Chronology of the Pali Canon: The case of the aorists (2002) — Noted the identity between MN 92 and Snp 3.7 and the role of the 32 marks.
- [Katre 1931] S. M. Katre, Early Buddhist Ballads and Their Relation to Older Upanishadic Literature (1931) — Analyzed the structure of the Sela Sutta as a fusion of the Keṇiya narrative from the Vinaya and additional verses of praise.
- [Lamotte 1988] Étienne Lamotte, History of Indian Buddhism (1988) — Noted the correspondence between the Pali Selasutta and the Sanskrit Śailagāthā.
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, History of Indian Literature, Vol. II (1933) — Discussed the textual borrowing and relationship between the Suttanipāta and Majjhimanikāya recensions.
- [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — Observed that page numbers embedded in translations of MN 92 refer to the PTS Sutta-nipāta edition.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pali Language and Literature (1994) — Reported the Divyāvadāna reference to Pūrṇa reciting the Śailagāthā alongside the Munigāthā and Arthavagga.
